rules: Hook in the first 3 seconds: the narrator says to the viewer, in second person, that one absurdly simple step already makes the everyday thing ('If you do X, you have a Y'). In the same shot a test character or object uses that crude version right away, so viewers wait for it to fail.

Build the whole video as a chain: failure, then 'so you' plus a fix, then the fix's real name. Each fix must cause or reveal the next failure. Use 4-6 links, and start each new failure with 'But'. Keep each link to 4-7 seconds so a small cliffhanger lands at least every 6 seconds.

Keep one locked wide set with a cutaway cross-section diagram in the lower half of the frame. Each fix adds, changes or reshapes a visible layer in that diagram, so progress stacks up like a build game. Cut away to a close or low shot only to show a failure, then return to the same wide framing.

Change the picture every 2-4 seconds: a new layer drops in, the weather or season turns, a machine rolls in, the camera cuts to a close-up, or a name card pops up. Each named technique gets a big text card the moment the narrator says it.

Escalate the enemies: start with an obvious everyday problem, then move to hidden ones (wear, time, season, scale). The last failure should be invisible from the surface and shown by zooming the cross-section to fill the frame.
Near the end, add one counterintuitive twist: the obvious culprit is not the real one. Back it with a single verifiable number on a big stat card in the form 'one X = N of Y'.

The narrator is the only voice: calm, matter-of-fact and a little dry, always talking to 'you'. Characters and machines act out the story without speaking. Use short, plain sentences with no hedging and no history lecture.

Payoff: finishing touches pop in, a cheeky named sign appears, and the narrator closes with 'Congratulations, you have built a ___.' The final wide shot matches the opening frame so the before and after reads at a glance and invites a rewatch.
In every line wrap 1-3 key words in *asterisks* (they render highlighted). No emoji.

rubric.check: Every number, unit and fact is correct and the arithmetic checks out; rounding is honest.
Every fix is triggered by a specific failure shown just before it, and every failure after the first comes from a real limit of the previous version. No step is just 'next you add'.
At least three fixes get their real technical name, said by the narrator right after the fix is shown and backed by a text card.
Each fix maps to a concrete visual change in the same cross-section or set, so a muted viewer can watch the object get better step by step.
The script opens and closes in second person ('you'), and the closing line congratulates the viewer on building the thing, matching the opening frame.
One late counterintuitive fact flips an obvious assumption and is shown as a single 'one X = N Y' stat card.
